1                        I.       WITNESS IDENTIFICATION

2    Q.   Please state your name and business address.

3    A.   My name is Alexander G. Trowbridge. I am the Director of Regulatory Pricing and

 4        Analysis at Southwestern Public Service Company (“SPS”), a subsidiary of Xcel

 5        Energy Inc. (“Xcel Energy”). My business address is 3500 Blake Street, Denver,

 6        Colorado 80205.

 7   Q.   On whose behalf are you testifying in this proceeding?

 8   A.   I am filing testimony on behalf of SPS, a New Mexico corporation and wholly

 9        owned electric utility subsidiary of Xcel Energy.

10   Q.   Are you the same Alexander G. Trowbridge that filed direct testimony in this

11        proceeding on November 20, 2025?

12   A.   Yes.

13   Q.   Was Attachment AGT-BR2 prepared by you or under your supervision and

14        control?

15   A.   Yes.




                                               1
                                     Case No. 25-00079-UT
                                   Supplemental Testimony
                                              of
                                   Alexander G. Trowbridge

 1                           II.   SECOND BENCH REQUEST
 2   Q.   What is the purpose of this supplemental testimony?

 3   A.   The purpose of my supplemental testimony is to respond to the following Second

 4        Bench Request issued by the New Mexico Public Regulation Commission

 5        (“Commission”):

 6               “SPS uses a 12-CP cost allocation to determine the costs to assign to New
 7               Mexico retail customers. Why does SPS believe that a 12-CP is more
 8               appropriate allocation factor than an allocation factor that more closely
 9               aligns with [Southwest Power Pool’s Planning Reserve Margin], which
10               focuses only on winter and summer peaks?”
11   Q.   Why does SPS use a 12-CP allocation for production resources?

12   A.   SPS uses the 12-CP method because SPS’s system demand is relatively steady

13        throughout the year. SPS transitioned from a 3-CP to a 12-CP jurisdictional

14        allocator for production resources during the 2005–2006 timeframe. The change

15        was made because SPS satisfied the 12-CP FERC test, which evaluates the ratio of

16        summer-to-winter peak demands. Because SPS has a high load factor, meaning its

17        peak demands are relatively consistent throughout the year, the 12-CP method more

18        accurately reflects how SPS's system is used across all months. The system is not

19        driven only by a few extreme summer or winter peaks. This approach ensures that

20        all jurisdictions contribute to production costs in proportion to their monthly peak



                                               2
                                    Case No. 25-00079-UT
                                  Supplemental Testimony
                                             of
                                  Alexander G. Trowbridge

 1        demands throughout the entire year, rather than focusing on only a few peak

 2        months.

 3   Q.   Please describe the 12-CP method.

 4   A.   The 12-CP method allocates demand-related costs based on each jurisdiction’s

 5        average contribution to the system’s 12 monthly coincident peak demands. For each

 6        month, we identify the hour of highest system-wide load, measure each

 7        jurisdiction’s load at that time (Texas and New Mexico), and average those

 8        contributions to determine allocation factors. This produces a year-round view of

 9        responsibility.

10   Q.   What are the primary advantages of the 12-CP method?

11   A.   The 12-CP method provides greater stability by averaging contributions across all

12        12 monthly coincident peaks, reducing volatility from weather-driven anomalies

13        and minimizing cost-shifting risks. It better reflects year-round system planning

14        and usage for high load factor systems like SPS. It also enjoys broad regulatory

15        acceptance and precedent.




                                              3
                                    Case No. 25-00079-UT
                                  Supplemental Testimony
                                             of
                                  Alexander G. Trowbridge

1    Q.   What would a Southwest Power Pool Planning Reserve Margin (“PRM”) or

 2        8-CP (or PRM-aligned) approach look like?

3    A.   A Southwest Power Pool Planning Reserve Margin aligned method or 8-CP method

4         would focus on contributions to 8 selected coincident peaks, the summer (June–

5         September) and winter (December–March) months that align with Southwest

6         Power Pool’s PRM periods. A PRM-weighted 8-CP applies greater emphasis to the

7         winter months to reflect SPS’s resource procurement.

 8   Q.   What are the advantages of an 8-CP or PRM-aligned approach?

 9   A.   An 8-CP aligned with PRM periods offers a stronger focus on the specific months

10        driving capacity needs (summer and winter peaks), which can more precisely tie

11        costs to peak reliability requirements. It may better align with seasonal resource

12        procurement, particularly with SPS’s emphasis on winter obligations.

13   Q.   What are the months in which Southwest Power Pool requires Planning

14        Reserve Margins?

15   A.   Southwest Power Pool’s summer PRM months cover June through September. The

16        winter PRM months cover December through March.




                                              4
                                     Case No. 25-00079-UT
                                   Supplemental Testimony
                                              of
                                   Alexander G. Trowbridge

 1   Q.   Is the Southwest Power Pool considering changes to the PRM requirements?

 2   A.   Yes. SPP has implemented separate summer (June–September) and winter

 3        (December–March) PRM seasons. While stakeholder processes, including Loss of

 4        Load Expectation studies and Supply Adequacy Working Group discussions,

 5        continue to evaluate resource adequacy needs year-round — including potential

 6        issues in shoulder months — there is no active proposal at this time to expand PRM

 7        requirements to additional seasons covering every month of the year. SPS will

 8        monitor these developments closely.

9    Q.   What are the relative disadvantages or trade-offs between 12-CP and 8-

10        CP/PRM?

11   A.   While 12-CP provides greater stability and broader reflection of annual usage, it

12        may slightly under-weight the most critical peak months in highly seasonal

13        systems. Conversely, 8-CP can introduce more volatility if peak periods shift and

14        may spark debate over month selection or weighting. Neither is universally

15        superior; the choice depends on system load characteristics, planning practices, and

16        data.




                                                5
                                   Case No. 25-00079-UT
                                 Supplemental Testimony
                                            of
                                 Alexander G. Trowbridge

 1   Q.   Now that SPS’s wholesale generation services have ended as of May 31, 2026,

 2        could SPS consider an alternate method that aligns with the Southwest Power

 3        Pool Planning Reserve Margin?

 4   A.   Yes. With the termination of wholesale generation services, SPS is no longer

 5        required to obtain Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (“FERC”) approval to

 6        change its production jurisdictional allocator. However, any such change would

 7        require coordination and approval from the Public Utility Commission of Texas

 8        and support across SPS’s jurisdictions, which presents a meaningful regulatory

 9        hurdle.

10   Q.   Have you prepared an attachment that shows jurisdictional allocation

11        variations between 12-CP, 8-CP, and a PRM-weighted 8-CP?

12   A.   Yes. I have prepared Attachment AGT-BR2, which compares the jurisdictional

13        allocation results under a 12-CP, a straight 8-CP, and a PRM-weighted 8-CP

14        method. As shown in the attachment, a straight 8-CP allocates only 0.31% less to

15        New Mexico compared to a 12-CP, while a PRM-weighted 8-CP allocates only

16        0.25% less to New Mexico. This demonstrates that, regardless of the method

17        chosen, the resulting jurisdictional allocations are nearly identical to a 12-CP

18        allocation.


                                             6
                                     Case No. 25-00079-UT
                                   Supplemental Testimony
                                              of
                                   Alexander G. Trowbridge

 1   Q.   Does SPS recommend a change in jurisdictional allocation for production

 2        costs?

 3   A.   No. As demonstrated in Attachment AGT-BR2, the PRM-weighted 8-CP produces

 4        results that are virtually identical to a 12-CP allocation. Given the minimal

 5        difference, SPS does not believe a change is warranted at this time. The 12-CP

 6        method has been used consistently and remains appropriate for allocating

 7        production costs across jurisdictions. Additionally, the Southwest Power Pool may

 8        change the PRM construct in the future to include all twelve months of the year.

 9   Q.   Why is it important for all jurisdictions to agree on the fundamental cost

10        assignment methodology?

11   A.   Agreement on core methods like 12-CP (or an alternative) is essential to avoid

12        protracted disputes, cost-shifting risks, and inefficient regulatory outcomes.

13        Inconsistent methodologies across Texas and New Mexico can lead to double

14        recovery or unrecovered costs for shared assets, unstable rates, and uncertainty for

15        customers and investors, and challenges in multi-jurisdictional planning such as

16        resource adequacy and transmission. Consensus supports equitable, transparent

17        allocations that align with cost causation, benefiting all customers while facilitating

18        timely recovery of prudent investments.


                                                7
                                    Case No. 25-00079-UT
                                  Supplemental Testimony
                                             of
                                  Alexander G. Trowbridge

 1   Q.   How can such agreement on methodology be achieved?

 2   A.   Agreement is best achieved through:

 3        1. Collaborative stakeholder processes, including joint technical conferences,
 4           workshops, or working groups involving Public Utility Commission of Texas,
 5           NMPRC Staff, intervenors, and SPS to review load data, planning studies, and
 6           impacts.

 7        2. Data-driven analysis, such as the comparative results shown in Attachment
 8           AGT-BR2.

 9        3. Reliance on precedent and consistency, with gradualism where changes are
10           proposed.

11        4. Comprehensive settlement discussions in rate cases.

12        5. Ongoing coordination through forums like Southwest Power Pool’s Regional
13           State Committee.

14   Q.   Do Southwest Power Pool’s PRMs impact how SPS allocates transmission

15        costs?

16   A.   No. Transmission costs should continue to be allocated using a 12-CP method. SPS

17        has firm transmission service obligations that exist year-round, not just during

18        summer and winter peak periods. Additionally, SPS’s transmission costs are driven

19        by FERC wholesale load obligations and network integration transmission service

20        requirements, which are based on year-round peak demands. Diverging from a 12-

21        CP allocator for transmission would create a mismatch between jurisdictional and



                                                8
                                  Case No. 25-00079-UT
                                Supplemental Testimony
                                           of
                                Alexander G. Trowbridge

1        wholesale cost allocations, which would be inappropriate and inconsistent with

2        how transmission service is planned and provided.

3   Q.   Does this conclude your pre-filed supplemental testimony?

4   A.   Yes.
